title: Clinical and Omics Data Visualization in R
text:
Welcome
cliomicplot produces publication-ready clinical and multi-omics figures in R with a formula grammar and pre-configured journal styles. This handbook explains how to use the package for clinical trial reporting, high-dimensional omics profiling, systems biology network coupling, and multi-panel journal composite assembly.

title: Clinical and Omics Data Visualization in R
text:
Package Scope
The package addresses three visual bottlenecks in biomedical data science:

Clinical Trial Visualizations: Kaplan-Meier curves with aligned risk tables, competing risks cumulative incidence, hazard ratio forest plots, and oncology patient response trajectories (RECIST waterfall and swimmer plots).
High-Throughput Omics: Volcano plots with biomarker callout boxes, differential expression contrast matrices, gene set enrichment running scores, microbiome GWAS Manhattan plots, and taxonomic abundance bubble matrices.
Systems Biology & Multi-Network Coupling: Cross-condition module comparison, comparative multi-group network graphs, modular circular networks coupled with peripheral environmental heatmaps, module preservation testing (Z_{\text{summary}}), and topological attack simulations.

title: 1  Graphic Grammar and Core API
text:
1.1 Formula Syntax
cliplot() provides a single entry point for generating biomedical visualizations through a formula syntax. This chapter details the formula grammar, the parameter system (clipar), and the type dispatch architecture.
cliplot() accepts standard R formulas mapping variables to visual roles:

title: 1  Graphic Grammar and Core API
text:
y ~ x: Bivariate plots (boxplots, scatter plots, violin plots, ROC curves).
y ~ x | facet: Conditioned plots faceted across biological subgroups or clinical trial cohorts.
Surv(time, event) ~ arm: Time-to-event outcomes with survival curves, risk tables, and hazard ratios.
~ x: Univariate distributions (histograms, density estimates, rank-abundance curves).

p <- cliplot(
  formula = Value ~ Biomarker,
  data    = clinical_data,
  type    = "boxplot",
  preset  = "nature"
)

title: 1  Graphic Grammar and Core API
text:
1.2 Function Dispatch and Plot Types
The type argument selects the geometry and statistical layer. It accepts either character aliases or typed constructor functions:


Code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

# Generate reproducible clinical cohort
set.seed(42)
df_cohort <- data.frame(
  Biomarker = factor(rep(c("Control", "Mild_AD", "Severe_AD"), each = 40)),
  IL13_pg_ml = c(rnorm(40, 4.2, 1.1), rnorm(40, 8.5, 1.8), rnorm(40, 15.2, 2.9)),
  Age_Group  = factor(rep(c("Pediatric", "Adult"), 60))
)

# Direct character specification
p_box <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data   = df_cohort,
  type   = "boxplot",
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Serum IL-13 by Clinical Severity"
)
p_box










1.2.1 Typed Constructor Functions
Constructor functions configure geometry-specific options with autocomplete support:


Code
p_viol <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data  = df_cohort,
  type  = type_violin(add_boxplot = TRUE, trim = FALSE),
  theme = "lancet"
)
p_viol

1.3 The Parameter Object: clipar()
clipar() sets visual attributes including line widths, point sizes, alpha transparency, jitter jitter-width, and label font sizes:


Code
pars <- clipar(
  point_size  = 2.2,
  line_width  = 0.9,
  alpha       = 0.75,
  font_size   = 10
)

p_custom <- cliplot(
  IL13_pg_ml ~ Biomarker,
  data   = df_cohort,
  type   = "beeswarm",
  params = pars,
  preset = "science"
)
p_custom

cliplot() objects are ggplot2 instances. You can extend them using the standard + operator or the cliplot_add() helper:

p_final <- p_box +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#B22222", linewidth = 0.6) +

2.1 Journal Themes Overview
Scientific journals impose strict typographic, dimensional, and contrast guidelines on submitted figures. cliomicplot provides journal theme presets and an automated verification gate (cli_scifig_qa) enforcing submission rules.

library(cliomicplot)

set.seed(101)
demo_df <- data.frame(

  Response  = c(rnorm(25, 20, 5), rnorm(25, 45, 6), rnorm(25, 78, 8))
)

p_nat <- cliplot(Response ~ Biomarker, data = demo_df, type = "boxplot", preset = "nature", title = "Nature Style")
p_lan <- cliplot(Response ~ Biomarker, data = demo_df, type = "boxplot", preset = "lancet", title = "Lancet Style")

title: 3  Survival Analysis and Time-to-Event Graphics
text:
3.1 Kaplan-Meier Curves: type = "km"
Time-to-event outcomes require specialized visual conventions. cliplot() implements Kaplan-Meier survival curves with aligned risk tables and Fine-Gray cumulative incidence curves for competing risks.
cliplot(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data, type = "km") estimates the survival function \hat{S}(t):
\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)
where d_i is the number of events and n_i is the number of individuals at risk at time t_i.
Code
library(cliomicplot)
library(survival)

set.seed(42)
n <- 120
surv_df <- data.frame(
  time   = rexp(n, rate = c(rep(0.03, 60), rep(0.06, 60))),
  status = sample(c(0, 1), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.8)),
  arm    = factor(rep(c("Targeted Therapy", "Standard of Care"), each = 60))
)

p_km <- cliplot(
  Surv(time, status) ~ arm,
  data   = surv_df,
  type   = "km",
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Overall Survival: Targeted Therapy vs Standard of Care"
)
p_km

title: 3  Survival Analysis and Time-to-Event Graphics
text:
3.2 Competing Risks Cumulative Incidence: type = "ci"
When competing events preclude the primary outcome (such as non-disease mortality in cancer trials), standard Kaplan-Meier estimates overestimate cumulative incidence. The subdistribution cumulative incidence function F_k(t) (Fine & Gray, 1999) accounts for competing causes:
F_k(t) = P(T \le t, C = k) = \int_0^t S(u-) d\Lambda_k(u)


Code
set.seed(88)
ci_df <- data.frame(
  time   = runif(100, 1, 36),
  event  = sample(0:2, 100, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.25)), # 0=Censor, 1=Relapse, 2=Non-Relapse Death
  arm    = factor(rep(c("Regimen A", "Regimen B"), each = 50))
)

p_ci <- cliplot(
  Surv(time, event) ~ arm,
  data   = ci_df,
  type   = type_km(cumulative_incidence = TRUE, risk_table = FALSE),
  preset = "science",
  title  = "Cumulative Incidence of Relapse with Competing Mortality"
)
p_ci

title: 4  Treatment Effects and Subgroup Forest Plots
text:
4.1 The Forest Plot Grammar: type = "forest"
Forest plots summarize treatment effects and evaluate consistency across patient subgroups in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. cliomicplot formats forest plots with tabular columns, logarithmic axes, and summary diamonds.
In clinical studies, treatment effect sizes (Hazard Ratios \text{HR}, Odds Ratios \text{OR}, or Relative Risks \text{RR}) are displayed on a logarithmic scale with 95% confidence intervals:
\log(\widehat{\text{HR}}) \pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}(\log(\widehat{\text{HR}}))
Code
library(cliomicplot)

# Reproducible clinical subgroup dataset
subgroup_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("Overall Population", "Age < 65", "Age >= 65", 
               "Female", "Male", "Stage III", "Stage IV"),
  HR       = c(0.68, 0.62, 0.76, 0.65, 0.71, 0.58, 0.79),
  CI_low   = c(0.54, 0.45, 0.55, 0.48, 0.53, 0.41, 0.59),
  CI_high  = c(0.85, 0.84, 1.04, 0.88, 0.95, 0.82, 1.06),
  P        = c(0.001, 0.003, 0.082, 0.006, 0.021, 0.002, 0.120)
)

p_forest <- cliplot(
  HR ~ Variable,
  data   = subgroup_df,
  type   = type_forest(
    ref_line    = TRUE,
    ref_val     = 1.0,
    log_scale   = TRUE,
    sort        = TRUE,
    stripe      = TRUE,
    show_values = TRUE
  ),
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Hazard Ratios for Progression-Free Survival Across Subgroups"
)
p_forest

title: 5  Oncology Trajectories: Waterfall and Swimmer Plots
text:
5.1 RECIST 1.1 Waterfall Plots: type = "waterfall"
Evaluating patient responses in oncology trials requires tracking both magnitude of tumor shrinkage (RECIST 1.1) and duration of response over time. cliomicplot provides waterfall, swimmer, and longitudinal trajectory visualizations.
Waterfall plots rank individual patients by the maximum percentage change in target lesion sum of longest diameters from baseline:
\Delta\% = \frac{\text{SLD}_{\text{post}} - \text{SLD}_{\text{baseline}}}{\text{SLD}_{\text{baseline}}} \times 100
Standard RECIST 1.1 thresholds define response categories: - Partial Response (PR): \Delta\% \le -30\% - Progressive Disease (PD): \Delta\% \ge +20\% - Stable Disease (SD): Between -30\% and +20\%
Code
library(cliomicplot)

set.seed(42)
n_pat <- 50
pat_ids <- paste0("PT-", sprintf("%03d", 1:n_pat))
shrinkage <- sort(rnorm(n_pat, mean = -15, sd = 35), decreasing = TRUE)
response <- ifelse(shrinkage <= -30, "PR",
            ifelse(shrinkage >= 20, "PD", "SD"))

wf_df <- data.frame(
  Patient  = factor(pat_ids, levels = pat_ids),
  Change   = shrinkage,
  Response = factor(response, levels = c("PD", "SD", "PR"))
)

p_wf <- cliplot(
  Change ~ Patient,
  data   = wf_df,
  type   = type_waterfall(
    response_thresholds = c("PD" = 20, "PR" = -30),
    bar_width           = 0.72
  ),
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Best Percentage Change in Target Lesion Size from Baseline"
)
p_wf

title: 5  Oncology Trajectories: Waterfall and Swimmer Plots
text:
5.2 Swimmer Plots: type = "swimmer"
Swimmer plots display the time on therapy for each patient, marked with milestones (time to first response, progression, or ongoing treatment):


Code
set.seed(123)
n_s <- 20
swim_df <- data.frame(
  Patient  = factor(paste0("PT-", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_s))),
  Months   = sort(runif(n_s, 3, 24)),
  Ongoing  = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), n_s, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.6)),
  Response = sample(c("Complete Response", "Partial Response", "Stable Disease"), n_s, replace = TRUE)
)

p_swim <- cliplot(
  Months ~ Patient,
  data   = swim_df,
  type   = type_swimmer(
    ongoing       = "Ongoing",
    bar_fill      = "Response",
    show_duration = TRUE,
    bar_linewidth = 4.0
  ),
  preset = "lancet",
  title  = "Duration of Response and Treatment Exposure"
)
p_swim

title: 6  Longitudinal Biomarkers and Clinical Meaningfulness (MCID)
text:
6.1 Multi-Protein Longitudinal Timecourses: type = "timecourse"
Statistical significance in biomarker changes does not automatically establish clinical benefit. This chapter covers multi-protein longitudinal timecourses and Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID) visualizations.
Monitoring multiple proteins across treatment cycles reveals pharmacodynamic kinetics:
Code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
time_pts <- c("Baseline", "Week 2", "Week 4", "Week 8", "Week 12")
proteins <- c("IL-13", "IL-22", "CCL17", "S100A9")

tc_df <- expand.grid(
  Time    = factor(time_pts, levels = time_pts),
  Protein = proteins
)
tc_df$Abundance <- c(
  # IL-13
  4.5, 3.8, 2.9, 1.8, 1.4,
  # IL-22
  3.2, 3.0, 2.4, 1.6, 1.2,
  # CCL17
  6.8, 5.1, 3.4, 2.2, 1.8,
  # S100A9
  5.4, 4.9, 4.0, 3.1, 2.7
)

p_tc <- cliplot(
  Abundance ~ Time | Protein,
  data   = tc_df,
  type   = "timecourse",
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Pharmacodynamic Suppression of Serum Inflammatory Biomarkers"
)
p_tc

title: 6  Longitudinal Biomarkers and Clinical Meaningfulness (MCID)
text:
6.2 Minimally Clinically Important Difference: type = "mcid"
The Minimally Clinically Important Difference (MCID) defines the smallest score change patients perceive as beneficial (e.g., a 4-point drop on the SCORAD scale or 0.5 standard deviation change):
\text{Responder} = \mathbb{I}(\Delta \text{Score}_i \ge \text{MCID})


Code
mcid_df <- data.frame(
  Endpoint = c("SCORAD Total (Biologic)", "Pruritus NRS (Topical)",
               "EASI-75 (Biologic)", "POEM Score (Biologic)",
               "DLQI Quality of Life (Placebo)"),
  Estimate = c(8.5, 3.4, 11.2, 4.2, 1.8),
  MCID     = c(5.0, 2.0,  8.0, 3.0, 4.0),
  N        = c(520, 380,  510, 240, 190),
  Category = c("Biologic Exceeding MCID", "Topical Exceeding MCID",
               "Biologic Exceeding MCID", "Biologic Exceeding MCID",
               "Placebo Below MCID")
)

p_mcid <- cliplot(
  Estimate ~ Endpoint,
  data   = mcid_df,
  type   = type_mcid(
    mcid          = "MCID",
    n_treated     = "N",
    category      = "Category",
    sort_by_ratio = TRUE
  ),
  preset = "lancet",
  title  = "Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) Evaluation",
  xlab   = "Absolute Clinical Estimate (|estimate|)"
)
p_mcid

title: 7  Differential Expression: Volcano Plots and DEG Contrasts
text:
7.1 Volcano Plots: type = "volcano"
High-throughput transcriptomics and proteomics evaluate thousands of features simultaneously. Volcano plots and contrast matrices map effect size (\log_2\text{FC}) against statistical significance (-\log_{10}P).
A volcano plot places \log_2(\text{Fold Change}) on the horizontal axis and -\log_{10}(P\text{-value}) or -\log_{10}(\text{FDR}) on the vertical axis:
\text{Significance Quadrants}: \begin{cases}
\text{Up-regulated}: & \log_2\text{FC} \ge \tau_{\text{FC}} \quad \text{and} \quad -\log_{10}(P) \ge \tau_P \\
\text{Down-regulated}: & \log_2\text{FC} \le -\tau_{\text{FC}} \quad \text{and} \quad -\log_{10}(P) \ge \tau_P \\
\text{Non-significant}: & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
Code
library(cliomicplot)

# Generate reproducible transcriptomics dataset
set.seed(42)
n_genes <- 1200
log2fc <- rnorm(n_genes, mean = 0, sd = 1.2)
pvals  <- runif(n_genes, 0, 1)^3 # Skew toward smaller p-values
gene_ids <- paste0("Gene_", 1:n_genes)

# Inject significant key biomarkers
key_markers <- c("IL13", "IL4R", "S100A7", "CCL18", "FLG", "LOR")
log2fc[1:6] <- c(3.2, 2.8, 4.1, 3.5, -3.8, -3.1)
pvals[1:6]  <- c(1e-12, 1e-9, 1e-15, 1e-11, 1e-14, 1e-10)
gene_ids[1:6] <- key_markers

volcano_df <- data.frame(
  Gene   = gene_ids,
  log2FC = log2fc,
  pValue = pvals
)

p_volc <- cliplot(
  pValue ~ log2FC,
  data   = volcano_df,
  type   = type_volcano(
    fc_cutoff   = 1.5,
    pval_cutoff = 0.01,
    label_genes = key_markers
  ),
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Transcriptomic Signature: Atopic Dermatitis Lesional vs Healthy Skin"
)
p_volc

7.2 DEG Contrast Matrices: type = "deg_compare"
Comparing differential expression across two distinct diseases or cohorts (e.g., AD vs HC compared against PSO vs HC) identifies shared versus disease-specific molecular pathways:

  FC_PSO ~ FC_AD,
  data   = compare_df,
  type   = "deg_compare",

title: 8  Pathway Enrichment: GSEA Running Enrichment Score Plots
text:
8.1 Mathematical Formulation of GSEA
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (Subramanian et al., PNAS 2005) evaluates whether an a priori defined gene set S shows cumulative enrichment at the extremes of a ranked gene list L. cliomicplot renders three-tiered GSEA figures.
Genes in L = \{g_1, g_2, \dots, g_N\} are ranked by differential expression metric r(g_j). The running enrichment score P_{\text{hit}}(S, i) walks down the ranked list:
P_{\text{hit}}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \in S, j \le i} \frac{|r_j|^p}{N_R}, \quad N_R = \sum_{g_j \in S} |r_j|^p
P_{\text{miss}}(S, i) = \sum_{g_j \notin S, j \le i} \frac{1}{N - N_H}
The Enrichment Score ES(S) is the maximum deviation of P_{\text{hit}} - P_{\text{miss}} from zero:
ES(S) = \arg\max_{i} |P_{\text{hit}}(S, i) - P_{\text{miss}}(S, i)|
Code
library(cliomicplot)

# Generate synthetic GSEA pathway enrichment results
set.seed(42)
pathways <- c(
  "Cytokine-Cytokine Receptor Interaction", "JAK-STAT Signaling Pathway",
  "Toll-like Receptor Signaling", "Th1 and Th2 Cell Differentiation",
  "Chemokine Signaling Pathway", "NF-kappa B Signaling",

Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) and Microbiome-GWAS (mGWAS) scan genetic variants across chromosomes for associations with clinical traits or microbial taxon abundances. cliomicplot provides Manhattan and dual-trait Miami plots.

title: 13  Central Networks Coupled with Multi-Domain Environmental Heatmaps

Central Network Ring (r \le 2.80): Contains modular network nodes, intra-module edge connections, cluster hulls, and radial module badges.
Annular Link Corridor (2.80 < r < 4.0): Separates the central network perimeter from the peripheral heatmaps. Outer boundary dots mark r \approx 3.38.
Corner Triangular Heatmaps: Four triangular correlation heatmaps occupy the corners. Diagonal indicator points connect via curved segments to central modules.

title: 13  Central Networks Coupled with Multi-Domain Environmental Heatmaps
text:
13.2 Layered Grammar of Graphics
The grammar separates coordinate computation from geometry rendering:

cli_env_network_data(): Computes spatial layouts, node positions, intra-module edges, cluster convex hulls, triangular heatmap coordinates, and link trajectories. Returns an S3 object of class cli_env_network_data.
geom_env_boundary(): Draws the circular boundary ring at r = 2.80 and the outer concentric dots at r \approx 3.38.
geom_env_central_network(): Draws central intra-module edges, cluster convex hulls, node glyphs (shape 16 fill-only), and module label badges.
geom_env_corner_heatmaps(): Draws triangular correlation tiles, significance asterisks or correlation values, diagonal connector points, 78° angled variable labels, and domain titles.
geom_env_links(): Draws curved inter-domain connecting lines weighted by significance and direction.
coord_env_network(): Enforces a 1:1 circular aspect ratio with standard viewport boundaries (xlim = c(-7.4, 7.4), ylim = c(-7.4, 7.4)).
theme_env_network(): Removes Cartesian grid lines and axis ticks while positioning a multi-tier publication legend.


13.2.1 Composing with the + Operator


Code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Generate grammatical data object
d <- cli_env_network_data(preset = "nature", show_values = TRUE)

# 2. Assemble plot layer by layer
p_grammar <- ggplot() +
  geom_env_boundary(data = d) +
  geom_env_central_network(data = d) +
  geom_env_corner_heatmaps(data = d) +
  geom_env_links(data = d) +
  coord_env_network() +
  theme_env_network(preset = "nature") +
  labs(title = "Layer-by-Layer Grammar Assembly (Nature Preset)")

14.1 Module Preservation Statistics (Z_{\text{summary}})
Assessing biological network changes between health and disease requires testing whether module structures persist and whether the network withstands random loss or targeted hub disruption.
cli_module_preservation() evaluates whether module density and intramodular hub rank are preserved between reference and test conditions under permutation testing (Langfelder et al., PLoS Comput Biol 2011).
crumbs: Part IV — Systems Biology and Coupled Multi-Network Architectures
14  Module Preservation and Targeted Attack Robustness

title: 14  Module Preservation and Targeted Attack Robustness
text:
14.1.1 Mathematical Definition of Z_{\text{summary}}
The composite preservation statistic Z_{\text{summary}} aggregates density and connectivity preservation metrics over B permutations:
Z_{\text{summary}} = \frac{Z_{\text{density}} + Z_{\text{connectivity}}}{2}
where Z_{\text{density}} evaluates whether features within module q maintain elevated mutual correlation and clustering in the test condition:
Z_{\text{density}} = \frac{Z_{\text{mean\_adj}} + Z_{\text{mean\_k}} + Z_{\text{cluster\_coef}} + Z_{\text{density\_raw}}}{4}
and Z_{\text{connectivity}} evaluates whether intramodular hub feature rankings are conserved between reference and test networks:
Z_{\text{connectivity}} = \frac{Z_{\text{kIM}} + Z_{\text{kME}}}{2}, \quad Z = \frac{\text{obs} - \mu_{\text{perm}}}{\sigma_{\text{perm}}}

Preservation Thresholds:

Z < 2 (dashed red line): No statistical evidence of module preservation.
2 \le Z \le 10 (dashed orange line): Moderate module preservation.
Z > 10 (dashed green line): Strong, statistically significant module preservation.




Code
library(cliomicplot)

demo_omics <- cli_demo_vitality_multiomics(n_samples = 35, n_features = 60, seed = 42)

pres_stats <- cli_module_preservation(
  ref_data    = demo_omics$ref_expr,
  test_data   = demo_omics$test_expr,
  ref_modules = demo_omics$modules,
  n_perm      = 100,
  seed        = 42
)

cliplot_module_preservation(
  pres_stats,
  title = "Cross-Network Module Preservation: WT Reference vs KO Test"
)

section: 14.2 Network Robustness and Targeted Attack Simulation
text:
14.2 Network Robustness and Targeted Attack Simulation
cli_network_robustness() simulates progressive network degradation under random node loss versus targeted attacks on high-degree hub nodes. cliplot_network_robustness() displays natural connectivity decay curves.

14.2.1 Mathematical Formulation of Natural Connectivity
Natural connectivity \bar{\lambda} derives from the spectrum of the network adjacency matrix A and reflects the redundancy of alternative paths between all node pairs (Wu et al., IEEE Trans Reliab 2012):
\bar{\lambda} = \ln \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N e^{\lambda_i} \right)
where \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_N are the eigenvalues of A. Natural connectivity strictly decreases monotonically as edges and nodes are removed, quantifying alternate path redundancy and topological stability.
The competitive-to-cooperative edge balance is evaluated as:
R_{\pm} = \frac{E_{-}}{E_{+}}


Code
rob_stats <- cli_network_robustness(
  networks     = demo_omics$networks,
  attack       = c("random", "degree"),
  rm_fractions = seq(0.05, 0.85, by = 0.05),
  n_perm       = 20,
  metric       = "natural_connectivity",
  seed         = 42
)

cliplot_network_robustness(
  rob_stats,
  title = "Network Robustness Under Progressive Node Removal"
)

title: 15  Empirical Linkage Engines and Permutation Testing
section: 15.2 Permutation Hypothesis Testing for Cross-Network Differences: cli_network_permutation()
text:
15.2 Permutation Hypothesis Testing for Cross-Network Differences: cli_network_permutation()
cli_network_permutation() tests whether global topological properties differ between experimental conditions. The function shuffles group assignments B times, re-estimates correlation networks on each permuted sample, and computes two-sided empirical P-values:
P_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}(|\Delta^{(b)}| \ge |\Delta^{\text{obs}}|)}{B + 1}
The tested metrics are edge density, natural connectivity \bar{\lambda}, negative-to-positive edge ratio R_{\pm}, mean degree, and clustering coefficient.


Code
# Stack reference and test samples
comm_combined <- rbind(demo_omics$ref_expr, demo_omics$test_expr)
group_combined <- rep(c("Reference_WT", "Perturbed_KO"),
                      c(nrow(demo_omics$ref_expr), nrow(demo_omics$test_expr)))

perm_res <- cli_network_permutation(
  comm_data  = comm_combined,
  group      = group_combined,
  ref_group  = "Reference_WT",
  test_group = "Perturbed_KO",
  cor_method = "spearman",
  cor_cutoff = 0.35,
  p_cutoff   = 0.05,
  n_perm     = 49,
  seed       = 42
)

title: 16  Assembling Multi-Panel Publication Composites
text:
16.1 The Double-Column Layout Standard
In peer-reviewed publications, individual analyses are assembled into unified, multi-panel composite figures. This chapter explains how to construct double-column figures conforming to Nature and Science standards using patchwork.
Leading journals specify standard column widths: - Single-Column: 89.0 mm (3.5 in) - 1.5-Column: 120.0\text{--}140.0 mm (4.7\text{--}5.5 in) - Double-Column: 183.0 mm (7.2 in)
patchwork combines separate ggplot2 instances while aligning plot axes and standardizing panel tags ((a), (b), (c)).

title: 16  Assembling Multi-Panel Publication Composites
text:
16.2 Assembling a 3-Panel Systems Biology Composite


Code
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Panel A: Node-level cross-network topology
demo_net <- generate_demo_cross_network()
p_a <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "nature",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Cross-Network Modular Architecture"
)

# Panel B: Module comparison overlap matrix
df_nodes <- data.frame(
  Feature     = paste0("Taxon_", 1:60),
  Discovery   = sample(c("M1_Barrier", "M2_Inflammation", "M3_Sebum"), 60, replace = TRUE),
  Replication = sample(c("ModA_Th2", "ModB_Stratum", "ModC_Lipid"), 60, replace = TRUE)
)
p_b <- cliplot(
  Replication ~ Discovery,
  data   = df_nodes,
  type   = type_module_compare(fill_by = "jaccard", show_stars = TRUE),
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Cross-Network Module Overlap"
)

# Panel C: Coupled environmental network
p_c <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Multi-Domain Environmental Coupling",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "nature",
  scifig             = TRUE
)

# Assemble using patchwork: Left column (A over B), Right column (C)
p_composite <- (p_a / p_b) | p_c
p_composite <- p_composite +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1.0, 1.25)) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "a",
    tag_prefix = "(",
    tag_suffix = ")",
    theme      = theme(
      plot.tag = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold", family = "sans")
    )
  )

p_composite

title: 17  Case Study: Biomarker Stratification and Dysbiosis in Atopic Dermatitis
text:
17.1 Clinical Background
Atopic Dermatitis (AD) involves epidermal barrier disruption, Type 2 immune polarization (IL-4/IL-13), and cutaneous Staphylococcus aureus colonization. This case study demonstrates an end-to-end analytical workflow combining transcriptomics, serum biomarkers, and microbial networks.
Patients present with varying disease severity evaluated by the SCORAD (Scoring Atopic Dermatitis) index. Transcriptomic profiling of lesional skin demonstrates upregulation of IL13, IL4R, CCL18, and S100A7, with concurrent downregulation of structural barrier genes FLG and LOR.

Code
library(cliomicplot)

set.seed(101)
n_genes <- 800
ad_volc_df <- data.frame(
  Gene   = paste0("Gene_", 1:n_genes),
  log2FC = rnorm(n_genes, 0, 1.3),
  pValue = runif(n_genes, 0, 1)^3
)

# Insert defined AD biomarkers
key_markers <- c("IL13", "IL4R", "CCL18", "S100A7", "FLG", "LOR")
ad_volc_df$log2FC[1:6] <- c(3.4, 2.9, 3.8, 4.2, -3.9, -3.2)
ad_volc_df$pValue[1:6] <- c(1e-12, 1e-9, 1e-11, 1e-15, 1e-14, 1e-10)
ad_volc_df$Gene[1:6]   <- key_markers

p_volc <- cliplot(
  pValue ~ log2FC,
  data   = ad_volc_df,
  type   = type_volcano(
    fc_cutoff   = 1.5,
    pval_cutoff = 0.01,
    label_genes = key_markers
  ),
  preset = "nature",
  title  = "Transcriptomic Signature: AD Lesional vs Healthy Controls"
)

18.1 Clinical Trial Background
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1 / anti-PD-L1) have altered treatment paradigms in solid tumors. This case study illustrates an integrated clinical trial reporting workflow combining survival outcomes, subgroup hazard ratios, and RECIST 1.1 response kinetics.
In a randomized Phase III trial evaluating anti-PD-1 immunotherapy versus standard chemotherapy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer, primary endpoints include Overall Survival (OS) and Objective Response Rate (ORR). Key predictive biomarkers include tumor PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Score (TPS: <1\%, 1\text{--}49\%, \ge 50\%).
